title: Aiding and Abetting
elements: The substantive offense was committed by some person.
The defendant associated with the criminal venture.
The defendant purposefully participated in the criminal venture.
The defendant sought by action to make that venture successful.
source: Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Aiding and Abetting (Agency); see also Rosemond v. United States, 572 U.S. 65 (2014) (advance knowledge required for the full scope of the offense).

title: Accessory After the Fact
elements: An offense against the United States was committed by another person.
The defendant knew that the offense had been committed.
With that knowledge, the defendant received, relieved, comforted, or assisted the offender in order to hinder or prevent the offender's apprehension, trial, or punishment.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 3 (statutory text); Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Accessory After the Fact.

title: Misprision of Felony
elements: A federal felony was committed by another person.
The defendant had actual knowledge of the commission of that felony.
The defendant failed to notify a federal judge or other federal authority as soon as possible.
The defendant took an affirmative step to conceal the felony.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 4 (statutory text); Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Misprision of Felony.

title: Conspiracy
aliases: Conspiracy to Defraud the United States
elements: Two or more persons made an agreement to commit an offense against the United States, or to defraud the United States or one of its agencies.
The defendant knew the unlawful purpose of the agreement and joined in it willfully, with the intent to further the unlawful purpose.
At least one of the conspirators, during the existence of the conspiracy, knowingly committed at least one overt act in furtherance of the object of the conspiracy.
source: Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Conspiracy (18 U.S.C. § 371).

title: Theft of Government Property (felony grade)
elements: The money or property described in the indictment belonged to the United States or an agency or department of the United States.
The defendant stole, embezzled, or knowingly converted the money or property to the defendant's own use or the use of another.
The defendant did so knowingly and willfully, with the intent to deprive the owner of the use or benefit of the money or property.
The value of the money or property exceeded $1,000 (element of the felony grade of the offense; theft of $1,000 or less is a lesser-included misdemeanor).
source: 18 U.S.C. § 641 (statutory text); Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Theft of Government Money or Property.

title: Unauthorized Retention of National Defense Information
aliases: Gathering, Transmitting, or Losing Defense Information
elements: The defendant had unauthorized possession of, access to, or control over a document, writing, photograph, or other tangible material relating to the national defense.

The information related to the national defense — that is, it was closely held by the government and its disclosure would be potentially damaging to the United States or useful to an enemy of the United States.

The defendant willfully retained the material and failed to deliver it to the officer or employee of the United States entitled to receive it, or willfully communicated, delivered, or transmitted it to a person not entitled to receive it.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 793(e) (statutory text); Gorin v. United States, 312 U.S. 19 (1941) (scope of 'national defense'). Note: this entry covers the tangible-materials prong. Where the charge rests on intangible 'information relating to the national defense,' the statute adds a scienter element — reason to believe the information could be used to the injury of the United States or to the advantage of any foreign nation. Other subsections of § 793 (e.g., (a)–(d), (f)) have different elements.

title: Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notification
elements: The defendant acted in the United States as an agent of a foreign government or foreign official — that is, the defendant agreed to operate within the United States subject to the direction or control of a foreign government or official.
The defendant failed to provide prior notification of that agency relationship to the Attorney General, as required by law.

The defendant acted knowingly — that is, the defendant knew he or she was acting in the United States as an agent of a foreign government or official and knew that prior notification had not been given to the Attorney General.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 951(a), (d) (statutory text); United States v. Rafiekian, 991 F.3d 529 (4th Cir. 2021) (agreement to operate subject to foreign direction or control). Note: § 951(d) excludes duly accredited diplomatic officers, certain officially acknowledged staff, and persons engaged in legal commercial transactions as defined by regulation.

title: False Statements
elements: The defendant made a statement or representation.
The statement or representation was false, fictitious, or fraudulent.
The false statement or representation was material.
The defendant made the statement or representation knowingly and willfully.
The statement or representation was made in a matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch of the United States.
source: Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), False Statement to a Federal Agency (18 U.S.C. § 1001); United States v. Gaudin, 515 U.S. 506 (1995) (materiality is a jury question). Note: § 1001(a)(1) (falsification/concealment by trick or scheme) and § 1001(a)(3) (false writings or documents) have parallel but distinct element sets.

title: Fraud in Connection with Means of Identification
elements: The defendant knowingly transferred, possessed, or used a means of identification of another person.
The defendant did so without lawful authority.
The defendant acted with the intent to commit, or to aid or abet, or in connection with, any unlawful activity that constitutes a violation of federal law or a felony under state or local law.

The offense satisfied the jurisdictional circumstance in § 1028(c) — for example, the means of identification was in or affected interstate or foreign commerce, or the mail was used in furtherance of the offense.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 1028(a)(7), (c) (statutory text). Note: § 1028(a) contains eight distinct offenses; subsections (a)(1)–(a)(6) and (a)(8) (production, transfer, and possession of identification documents and document-making implements) have different element sets.

title: Aggravated Identity Theft
jurisdiction: General (statutory text and Supreme Court case law)
elements: The defendant committed a predicate felony enumerated in § 1028A(c) (for example, wire fraud, mail fraud, bank fraud, or false statements).
During and in relation to that predicate felony, the defendant knowingly transferred, possessed, or used a means of identification of another person.
The defendant did so without lawful authority.
The defendant knew that the means of identification belonged to another actual person.
The misuse of the means of identification was at the crux of what made the underlying conduct criminal — not merely an ancillary feature of the predicate offense.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 1028A (statutory text); Flores-Figueroa v. United States, 556 U.S. 646 (2009) (knowledge that the identification belonged to a real person); Dubin v. United States, 599 U.S. 110 (2023) ('crux of the criminality' requirement).

title: Computer Fraud and Abuse — Unauthorized Access to Obtain Information
jurisdiction: General (statutory text and Supreme Court case law)
elements: The defendant intentionally accessed a computer without authorization, or exceeded authorized access — that is, accessed areas of the computer (files, folders, or databases) that were off-limits to the defendant.
By that access, the defendant obtained information.
The computer was a protected computer — one used in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce or communication.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2)(C), (e)(2), (e)(6) (statutory text); Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021) (scope of 'exceeds authorized access'). Note: § 1030(a) contains seven distinct offenses (e.g., (a)(4) access with intent to defraud, (a)(5) damage offenses) with different element sets, and felony grading of (a)(2) requires additional proof.

title: Mail Fraud
elements: The defendant knowingly devised or intended to devise a scheme to defraud — that is, a scheme to deprive another of money or property by means of materially false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises.
The defendant acted with the specific intent to defraud.
For the purpose of executing the scheme, the defendant mailed something, or caused it to be mailed, through the United States Postal Service or a private or commercial interstate carrier.
source: Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Mail Fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1341); Kelly v. United States, 590 U.S. 391 (2020) and Ciminelli v. United States, 598 U.S. 306 (2023) (object of the scheme must be traditional money or property).

title: Wire Fraud
elements: The defendant knowingly devised or intended to devise a scheme to defraud — that is, a scheme to deprive another of money or property by means of materially false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises.
The defendant acted with the specific intent to defraud.
For the purpose of executing the scheme, the defendant transmitted, or caused to be transmitted, a communication by wire, radio, or television in interstate or foreign commerce.
source: Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Wire Fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1343); Kelly v. United States, 590 U.S. 391 (2020) and Ciminelli v. United States, 598 U.S. 306 (2023) (object of the scheme must be traditional money or property).

title: Bank Fraud — Scheme to Defraud a Financial Institution
elements: The defendant knowingly executed, or attempted to execute, a scheme or artifice to defraud a financial institution.
The defendant acted with the intent to defraud.

The financial institution was a 'financial institution' within the meaning of federal law at the time of the offense (for example, a bank whose deposits were insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation).
source: Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Bank Fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1344); Shaw v. United States, 580 U.S. 63 (2016). Note: § 1344(2) (obtaining bank property by false pretenses) is a distinct offense — under Loughrin v. United States, 573 U.S. 351 (2014), it does not require intent to defraud the bank itself, but requires that the false statement be the mechanism for obtaining bank property.

title: Obstruction of Justice (Omnibus Clause)
jurisdiction: General (statutory text and Supreme Court case law)
elements: A judicial proceeding (including a grand jury proceeding) was pending.
The defendant knew of the pending judicial proceeding.
The defendant corruptly endeavored to influence, obstruct, or impede the due administration of justice in that proceeding.

The defendant's endeavor had a nexus to the proceeding — that is, a relationship in time, causation, or logic such that the endeavor had the natural and probable effect of interfering with the due administration of justice.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 1503(a) (omnibus clause, statutory text); United States v. Aguilar, 515 U.S. 593 (1995) (nexus requirement). Note: § 1503 also contains separate clauses protecting jurors and court officers, with different elements.

title: Witness Tampering — Influencing Testimony
jurisdiction: General (statutory text and Supreme Court case law)
elements: The defendant knowingly used intimidation, threatened, or corruptly persuaded another person, or engaged in misleading conduct toward another person, or attempted to do so.
The defendant acted with the intent to influence, delay, or prevent the testimony of any person in an official proceeding.

Where the charge rests on corrupt persuasion, the defendant acted with consciousness of wrongdoing, and contemplated a particular official proceeding in which the testimony might be given (the proceeding need not have been pending or about to be instituted at the time of the offense).
source: 18 U.S.C. § 1512(b)(1), (f)(1) (statutory text); Arthur Andersen LLP v. United States, 544 U.S. 696 (2005) (consciousness of wrongdoing and nexus for 'knowingly ... corruptly persuades'). Note: § 1512 contains many distinct offenses — (a) killing or physical force, (b)(2)–(3) other tampering objects, (c) obstruction of official proceedings (see Fischer v. United States, 603 U.S. 480 (2024), limiting § 1512(c)(2)), and (d) harassment — each with different elements.

title: Destruction, Alteration, or Falsification of Records in Federal Investigations
jurisdiction: General (statutory text and Supreme Court case law)
elements: The defendant knowingly altered, destroyed, mutilated, concealed, covered up, falsified, or made a false entry in a record, document, or tangible object.

The defendant acted with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence the investigation or proper administration of a matter within the jurisdiction of a department or agency of the United States, or in relation to or contemplation of any such matter or case.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (statutory text); Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015) ('tangible object' is limited to objects used to record or preserve information).

title: Economic Espionage
elements: The defendant knowingly stole, or without authorization appropriated, took, carried away, concealed, copied, duplicated, downloaded, transmitted, delivered, received, bought, possessed, or otherwise misappropriated information, or attempted or conspired to do so (in the manner charged in the indictment).

The information was a trade secret — the owner took reasonable measures to keep it secret, and it derived independent economic value from not being generally known to, or readily ascertainable by, the public.
The defendant knew the information was a trade secret (proprietary information that the owner sought to protect).
The defendant intended or knew that the offense would benefit a foreign government, foreign instrumentality, or foreign agent.
source: 18 U.S.C. §§ 1831(a), 1839(3) (statutory text). Note: where the charge is receipt or purchase under § 1831(a)(3), the government must also prove the defendant knew the trade secret was stolen or appropriated without authorization.

title: Theft of Trade Secrets
elements: The defendant knowingly stole, or without authorization appropriated, took, carried away, concealed, copied, duplicated, downloaded, transmitted, delivered, received, bought, possessed, or otherwise misappropriated information, or attempted or conspired to do so (in the manner charged in the indictment).

The information was a trade secret — the owner took reasonable measures to keep it secret, and it derived independent economic value from not being generally known to, or readily ascertainable by, the public.
The defendant knew the information was a trade secret.
The trade secret was related to a product or service used in or intended for use in interstate or foreign commerce.
The defendant intended to convert the trade secret to the economic benefit of anyone other than the owner.
The defendant intended or knew that the offense would injure the owner of the trade secret.
source: 18 U.S.C. §§ 1832(a), 1839(3) (statutory text). Note: where the charge is receipt or purchase under § 1832(a)(3), the government must also prove the defendant knew the trade secret was stolen or appropriated without authorization.

title: Money Laundering — Concealment
elements: The defendant conducted or attempted to conduct a financial transaction.
The financial transaction involved the proceeds of a specified unlawful activity.
The defendant knew that the property involved in the transaction represented the proceeds of some form of unlawful activity.

The defendant knew that the transaction was designed in whole or in part to conceal or disguise the nature, the location, the source, the ownership, or the control of the proceeds of the specified unlawful activity.
source: Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Laundering Monetary Instruments (18 U.S.C. § 1956); Cuellar v. United States, 553 U.S. 550 (2008) (transaction must be designed to conceal, not merely have the effect of concealing). Note: § 1956 contains multiple distinct offenses — promotion (a)(1)(A)(i), tax (a)(1)(A)(ii), avoidance of reporting (a)(1)(B)(ii), international transportation (a)(2), and sting transactions (a)(3) — each with different elements.

title: Monetary Transactions in Criminally Derived Property
aliases: Monetary Transactions in Criminally Derived Property
elements: The defendant knowingly engaged or attempted to engage in a monetary transaction.
The monetary transaction involved criminally derived property of a value greater than $10,000.
The property was derived from a specified unlawful activity.
The defendant knew that the property was criminally derived (the defendant need not have known it was derived from a specified unlawful activity).
The offense took place in the United States, or the defendant was a United States person as defined by law.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 1957(a), (c), (d), (f) (statutory text); Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Criminal Cases) (2019), Engaging in Monetary Transactions in Property Derived from Specified Unlawful Activity.

title: Providing Material Support to Terrorists
elements: The defendant provided material support or resources, or concealed or disguised the nature, location, source, or ownership of material support or resources, or attempted or conspired to do so.

The defendant knew or intended that the material support or resources were to be used in preparation for, or in carrying out, a violation of one of the federal offenses enumerated in § 2339A(a), or in preparation for, or in carrying out, the concealment of an escape from the commission of any such violation.
source: 18 U.S.C. §§ 2339A(a), 2339A(b) ('material support or resources' defined) (statutory text).

title: Providing Material Support to a Designated Foreign Terrorist Organization
jurisdiction: General (statutory text and Supreme Court case law)
aliases: Material Support to Designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations
elements: The defendant knowingly provided material support or resources to a foreign terrorist organization, or attempted or conspired to do so.
The organization was designated as a foreign terrorist organization at the time of the offense.

The defendant knew that the organization was a designated foreign terrorist organization, or knew that the organization had engaged or was engaging in terrorist activity or terrorism (as those terms are defined by law).

A jurisdictional basis under § 2339B(d) existed — for example, the offense occurred in whole or in part within the United States, or the defendant was a national of the United States or was otherwise subject to United States jurisdiction as specified in the statute.
source: 18 U.S.C. § 2339B(a)(1), (d), (g) (statutory text); Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, 561 U.S. 1 (2010) (knowledge requirement; coordination with the organization distinguishes support from independent advocacy).
